answer.rationale: Finance mandates an 18% cut and the incumbent has already refused to reopen price this cycle, so negotiate_terms and renew_incumbent are closed paths. Deferring the decision is not viable because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew and the assembly line is at 94% utilization with no buffer — any gap in supply becomes an immediate delivery-risk event. That leaves switch_primary_vendor and add_second_source as the two viable directions, and I must choose exactly one. Memory c2 records that the low-cost vendor was used as primary supply last year: onboarding was quick, invoicing was accurate, and the unit-cost reduction was sharp. That is direct, relevant evidence that the vendor can absorb a primary-supply role without the kind of migration friction that memory c1 warns about for the incumbent relationship. Memory c1 confirms that staying with the incumbent avoided migration work and delivery interruption — but the incumbent's refusal to move on price, combined with the 18% mandate, makes renewal untenable this cycle; the integration stability it preserved is now a luxury the budget cannot afford. The low-cost vendor's quote alone meets the mandate, which means no second-source hedge is needed to hit the number, and adding a second source (memory c3) would address a concentration risk that is secondary to the immediate cost-and-continuity problem. One sourcing decision this cycle; I spend it where it resolves both constraints simultaneously: switching primary supply to the quoted low-cost vendor secures the 18% reduction and locks in continuity before the 14-day expiry, with the onboarding path already proven by c2. I will flag for the next review cycle: re-introduce a second source for the constrained component and revisit the incumbent for a multi-year volume play once the budget pressure eases.
